lead: At collapse, a reinforced concrete section is idealised by a rectangular stress block. IS 456 replaces the curved concrete compression stress with an average stress 0.36fck over the compression depth xu. This gives one force C and one lever arm z, so moment capacity is C z. The idea makes flexural design quick and consistent. It is used for singly reinforced beams and slabs. Only a few universities teach the parameters in this detail.
prereq: You need: characteristic strength from 1.5 and design values from 1.6.

blocks.text: At the limit state of collapse in flexure, concrete near the top fibre is at its design compressive strength. The real stress distribution is curved. IS 456 permits an equivalent rectangular block. Here b is the section width in mm, d is the effective depth in mm, and xu is the neutral axis depth in mm. The equivalent block is uniform at 0.36fck over depth xu, where fck is the characteristic cube strength in N/mm². The real curved distribution that it replaces has its peak 0.446fck (= 0.67fck/1.5) at the extreme compression fibre, and this shape is what fixes the centroid at 0.42xu. The numbers 0.36 and 0.42 are the stress block parameters. 0.36 is the average stress coefficient; 0.42 fixes the centroid. The 0.36fck is the average intensity over the compression zone, while the 0.42xu position of the resultant is fixed by the real curved shape; together they are the code's idealisation, not two independent facts about a uniform stress.

blocks.where: C is compressive force in N; fck is characteristic concrete strength in N/mm²; b is width in mm; xu is neutral axis depth in mm.

blocks.text: Compression C acts at 0.42xu from the top fibre. Steel tension T acts at the steel centroid, at effective depth d. The lever arm is z = d − 0.42xu. For horizontal equilibrium, T = C. The design steel force is T = 0.87fy Ast, where fy is characteristic yield strength in N/mm² and Ast is tension steel area in mm². The moment capacity about either force is Mu = C z. In a singly reinforced rectangular section at collapse, these equations give the whole flexural check: C from concrete, z from geometry, and Ast from force balance.

blocks.where: z is lever arm in mm; d is effective depth in mm; xu is neutral axis depth in mm.

blocks.text: Mu = C z = 0.36 fck b xu (d − 0.42xu)
blocks.where: Mu is moment capacity in Nmm; C is compressive force in N; z is lever arm in mm.

figure.caption: The section at xu gives C and z; their product is Mu, and C = 0.87fyAst gives the steel area.

spec.title: Stress block parameters at collapse
spec.aria: A flow from the section to compression force and lever arm, then to moment capacity, with steel area from force balance.

examples.question: A singly reinforced rectangular beam has b = 230 mm, d = 450 mm, M25 concrete and Fe415 steel. Take xu = 0.48d. Find C, z, Mu and Ast at collapse.
steps: 0.48 is the limiting xu/d for Fe415 steel, so the section is at Mu,lim. xu = 0.48d = 0.48 × 450 = 216 mm.
examples.answer: C = 447,120 N, z = 359.28 mm, Mu ≈ 160.6 kNm and Ast ≈ 1238 mm² (about 1240 mm²; provide 4 bars of 20 mm).
examples.check:
fck=25.0
fy=415.0
b=230.0
d=450.0
xu=0.48*d
C=0.36*fck*b*xu
z=d-0.42*xu
Mu=C*z/1e6
Ast=C/(0.87*fy)
print(f"{C:.0f}")
print(f"{z:.2f}")
print(f"{Mu:.1f}")
print(f"{Ast:.0f}")

traps: Writing C = 0.446fck b xu, that is, using the peak stress over the full depth xu, overestimates compression; 0.446fck is only the peak of the real distribution, not its average.
Writing z = d − 0.42d or z = 0.58d; the correct term is 0.42xu, so z = d − 0.42xu.
Adding C and T instead of equating them; at collapse T = C.
Applying another partial safety factor to 0.36 or 0.87; these coefficients already carry material safety.
Measuring xu or 0.42xu from the steel instead of the extreme compression fibre.

quiz.a: xu is the depth of the concrete compression zone from the extreme compression fibre at collapse, in mm.

quiz.q: State the two IS 456 stress block parameters used in flexure.
quiz.a: Average stress coefficient 0.36 and centroid coefficient 0.42.

quiz.q: Why is 0.446fck not used as the average stress in C?
quiz.a: The real block is curved; 0.446fck is peak. The equivalent rectangle uses average 0.36fck over xu. Using 0.446 would overestimate C.

quiz.q: For fck = 30 N/mm², b = 300 mm and xu = 120 mm, find C.
A section has d = 500 mm, xu = 200 mm and C = 600 kN. Find z and Mu.
Why must C equal T at collapse?
quiz.a: At collapse C and T must balance to prevent net axial force. Setting C = T gives Ast. If C ≠ T, the assumed xu is wrong for that steel area.

quiz.q: A student computes C = 0.446fck b xu. Is this correct for the IS 456 equivalent block? Explain.
quiz.a: No. 0.36fck is the average over xu. 0.446fck is peak; using it over full xu overestimates C and Mu.

beyond: Not for the exam. Design offices use spreadsheets and BIM tools that encode the same block. Researchers compare IS 456 with Eurocode 2 and ACI 318 stress blocks, especially for high-strength concrete. Strain compatibility and parabolic-rectangular curves matter for nonlinear analysis.
